extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic; philosophers; readers seeking a systematic account of reasoning and the analysis of language
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook treatment that defines the province of logic, argues for beginning with an analysis of language (names), and analyzes the structure and role of propositions and inference. It aims to produce practical canons for testing sufficiency of evidence and distinguishing correct from incorrect reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of Logic: guidance of one's own thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole object of Logic is the guidance of one's own thoughts; the communication of those thoughts to others falls under Rhetoric or Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic is to be restricted to operations that conduce to our own knowledge and command over that knowledge for our own uses. Do not conflate logical analysis with rhetorical aims or pedagogical transmission. Evaluation of arguments should focus on internal guidance of thought (clarity, sufficiency of evidence, correctness of inference) rather than on persuasive devices or educational methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish truths by mode of knowing: intuition vs inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths are known in two ways: some directly (intuition or consciousness), some through other truths (inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic is concerned primarily with truths known by inference, not with those known immediately by consciousness. Examples: bodily sensations and mental feelings are intuitive and not subject to logical proof; historical events or theorems of mathematics are inferred from premises. Beware the error of treating immediate consciousness as needing logical proof. Also beware apparent intuitions that are really rapid inferences (e.g., perception of distance involves rapid experiential inference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic is the science of Proof/Evidence, not of Belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is not the science of Belief, but the science of Proof, or Evidence. It furnishes a test for ascertaining whether or not a belief is well grounded insofar as belief professes to be founded upon proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, apply logical criteria to the evidence and the relation between evidence and conclusions. Logic supplies principles and canons for testing sufficiency of evidence; it does not itself supply empirical facts or subject-matter content. The judge should ask whether the evidence legitimately supports the asserted belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: logic judges relations between data and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic points out to what conditions all facts must conform in order that they may prove other facts; it cannot, by itself, show that fact A proves fact B, but indicates the conditions under which such proof holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect logic to teach particular empirical symptoms, rules of art, or domain-specific facts (e.g., what symptoms indicate violent death). Instead use logic to assess whether the observations and rules of a particular field suffice to justify a conclusion. The evaluation separates domain knowledge (which provides evidence) from logical principles (which evaluate the evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include analysis of language (Naming, Definition, Classification) within logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic includes the operation of Naming; for language is an instrument of thought. It also includes Definition and Classification as auxiliary to inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before analyzing propositions or inferences, scrutinize names and linguistic usages because imperfections or misuses of language are a fertile source of error. The analysis of the instruments (words, names, definitions) used in investigation is part of logical analysis. Evaluate whether terms are used consistently and whether classifications and definitions serve to make evidence and conclusions accessible and less error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of commencing with an analysis of names
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry into language, so far as is needful to guard against errors it gives rise to, has at all times been deemed a necessary preliminary to the science of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start logical inquiry by clarifying the meaning and right use of various kinds of words. This prevents distortions in subsequent reasoning. Practical instruction: enumerate and examine the ordinary-usage distinctions that names introduce, because they bring before us the collective intelligence's recognized distinctions, which is essential for a comprehensive analysis of propositional possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a proposition: subject, predicate, copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition consists of three parts: the Subject, the Predicate, and the Copula. A proposition is discourse in which something is affirmed or denied of something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing propositions, identify the subject (that of which something is affirmed/denied), the predicate (that which is affirmed/denied), and the copula (the sign of affirmation/denial). Examples: 'Gold is yellow' (predicate = yellow, subject = gold, copula = is). Clear parsing of propositions is foundational to testing inference and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief as relation of two objects (two names required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest act of belief supposes two objects (two names): one of them is not sufficient by itself to be an object of belief; belief requires something affirmed or denied of something else (e.g., 'the sun' vs 'the sun exists').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat single names as propositions that call for belief. To form a belief one must assert something (e.g., existence, possession of a quality) of a subject. Examples: 'the sun' alone does not invite belief; 'the sun exists' does. Anti-pattern: assuming that naming an object implies an asserted proposition about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with propositions to discover what questions are conceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer to every question which it is possible to frame is contained in a Proposition; to know what inquiries are conceivable examine the varieties of propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze proposition-forms to map the space of possible questions and judgments. This helps determine what kinds of evidence and inference rules will be needed. Practical use: classify proposition-types to ensure your logical analysis covers the variety of conceivable inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analytical depth to that required for practical detection of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to decompose mental operations into their ultimate elements beyond the point necessary for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes; leave more minute analysis to metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical logic (an art useful to inquirers), analyze reasoning only to the extent that inaccuracies become visible and testable. Analogy: one needn't fully dissect muscular anatomy to learn bodily exercises except where defects require it. This prescribes a pragmatic boundary: go as deep as needed for reliable correction and testing, no further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame canons/rules for testing sufficiency of any given evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal object is, on the foundation of analysis of reasoning, to bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deliverable of logical analysis should include explicit canons for assessing evidence-conclusion relationships. These canons should be practical, derived from the analysis of inference and subordinate operations (naming, definition, classification). Use examples and counterexamples to illustrate application and failure of the canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-based enumeration captures collective distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is preferable to begin with names so as to bring before us the distinctions recognized by ordinary language and by the collective intelligence of mankind, rather than from an idiosyncratic enumeration of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cataloguing kinds of things or distinctions, start from ordinary linguistic categories to avoid omission of distinctions recognized broadly. Later you may abridge or collapse distinctions found to be non-fundamental. Do not assume a priori that ordinary language multiplies varieties unnecessarily; first record them, then evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that rapid inferences can masquerade as intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth which is really the result of a very rapid inference may seem to be apprehended intuitively; e.g., perception of distance by the eye is an inference grounded on experience though it feels intuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a judgment is intuitive or inferential, consider whether a rapid, experience-based comparison or inference underlies the apparent intuition. This affects whether logic applies: if perception involves inference it falls within logic's province; if truly intuitive, it does not. Use such diagnostic examples to decide applicability of logical testing.
